story.title: Increase daily payment limits for premium customers
story.description: Increase daily payment limits for premium customers from AED 25,000 to AED 50,000 for domestic transfers. The payment-service must obtain premium eligibility and the effective account limit from account-service before accepting each payment. Keep fraud screening active through fraud-engine and use the transaction ledger in transaction-db to calculate the remaining daily allowance, including concurrent requests. Roll out the business rule behind an approved feature flag during the payments release window. Operations must confirm threshold monitoring and rollback readiness before enabling the higher limit; standard customer limits remain unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: A premium account can submit domestic payments totaling AED 50,000 per bank-local calendar day; the next payment is declined.
A standard account retains its AED 25,000 daily limit and existing per-payment checks.
Concurrent payment submissions cannot exceed the account daily limit, and retries create one transaction ledger posting.
Every accepted payment passes fraud screening; operations approves monitoring and can restore the previous limit with the feature flag.

findings.text: The change makes payment-service read premium eligibility and the effective account limit from account-service before accepting a payment (for example via account-service.limits-read). notification-service sits downstream of payment-service and delivers consent-aware messages to verified destinations. Higher-limit premium customers may generate different notification content or volume, so consent state, channel preferences and destination verification should be re-checked against the new behaviour.

Feature-flag toggling introduces differentiated treatment by premium status and can create new log and audit entries. Exposure exists if those records, or the limit/eligibility responses, retain or disclose more personal data than the purpose requires.

Verify access controls and privacy regression tests covering the new cross-service calls between payment-service and account-service, including account-service.limits-read.
Confirm that new limit, eligibility and flag-related logging on payment-service, account-service and transaction-db excludes personal data that is not needed for the stated purpose.

Remaining daily allowance is computed from transaction-db ledger reads, such as transaction-db.daily-total, and must remain accurate under concurrent requests. Weakness in that read or in the concurrency handling would affect both limit enforcement and ledger reconciliation.

Raising the limit changes the population and value range of payments routed to fraud-engine screening. Coverage, rule thresholds and audit records for the higher-value band should be reconfirmed so screening evidence remains complete.

transaction-db posts balanced entries and replicates change data to the reporting store. The change should be checked to confirm that posting integrity, idempotency and downstream reporting reconciliation are unaffected by the new limit logic.

The notification-service may use the secondary email only after verification and explicit customer consent. Existing retention, access, correction and erasure controls extend to both new fields, and consent evidence is recorded for GDPR review.

Existing retention, access, correction and erasure processes are applied to both fields, and consent evidence is retained for GDPR review. Legal name and primary email paths are untouched, including blank-value handling.

story.title: Card freeze/unfreeze in mobile app with step-up authentication
story.description: Add card freeze/unfreeze controls to the mobile app through a new API gateway endpoint backed by card-service. Each card status change requires step-up authentication from authentication-service, binds the proof to the device and requested action, and exposes only masked card details. Update mobile-banking and api-gateway authorization policies together with the card control flow. PCI DSS review and security sign-off are outstanding: the prototype permits cross-device proof replay and lacks fail-closed verification evidence. These unresolved authentication defects and the missing rollback rehearsal are release blockers until the acceptance criteria have demonstrated evidence.
acceptance_criteria: A cardholder can freeze or unfreeze their own card in mobile-banking through the API gateway endpoint, and the refreshed view shows the confirmed status.
Each action requires a fresh step-up proof bound to the card, device and requested action; replay and cross-customer requests are rejected.
If authentication-service is unavailable or proof validation fails, card-service leaves the card status unchanged and denies the action.
Card control traces contain masked identifiers only; PCI DSS review, security sign-off and a rehearsed rollback are mandatory before release.

requirement.business_summary: Cardholders gain the ability to freeze or unfreeze their own card from the mobile app. Every card status change requires a fresh step-up authentication proof bound to the card, device and requested action, and only masked card details are exposed. Replay and cross-customer requests must be rejected, and if authentication is unavailable or proof validation fails the card status must remain unchanged. PCI DSS review, security sign-off and a rehearsed rollback are outstanding release blockers.
requirement.technical_summary: A new API Gateway endpoint backs card freeze/unfreeze calls from Mobile Banking into Card Service. Authentication Service must supply a fresh step-up proof bound to card, device and requested action; Card Service must fail closed (leave status unchanged, deny action) when authentication is unavailable or proof validation fails. Mobile Banking and API Gateway authorization policies are updated along with the card control flow, and card control traces must carry masked identifiers only. The current prototype permits cross-device proof replay and lacks fail-closed verification evidence; no rollback rehearsal has been performed.

story.title: Fraud rule update: velocity check for card-not-present payments
story.description: Update the fraud rule in fraud-engine to add a rolling velocity check for card-not-present payments. The payment-service must supply the existing payment event attributes and apply the returned screening decision before posting. The risk engine provides the current policy signal used when the threshold is exceeded. Block the sixth attempt for the same card token within a rolling sixty-second window, including declined attempts. This change shares the payment screening path and core-payments deployment with ST-101, so both stories must agree on rule ordering, combined regression coverage and rollout timing.
acceptance_criteria: The first five card-not-present attempts for one card token inside sixty seconds are evaluated normally; the sixth is blocked by the velocity rule.
Declined attempts count toward the velocity window, while distinct card tokens maintain independent counters.
fraud-engine includes the active risk-engine policy signal and rule version in its screening decision.
Combined ST-101 and ST-110 regression evidence confirms premium payment limits cannot bypass fraud screening; their core-payments release order is agreed.

requirement.business_summary: Card-not-present payments will be screened by a new rolling velocity rule: the first five attempts on a single card token within sixty seconds are evaluated normally, and the sixth is blocked. Declined attempts count toward the window, while each distinct card token keeps its own counter. The rule supports the existing premium payment limit controls rather than replacing them, so limit checks cannot be bypassed by fraud screening.
requirement.technical_summary: The fraud-engine rule set gains a rolling sixty-second velocity counter keyed by card token for card-not-present payment events, counting declined attempts and blocking the sixth attempt. The screening decision returned by fraud-engine continues to be applied by payment-service before posting, and fraud-engine now includes the active risk-engine policy signal and the rule version in that decision. Rule ordering, combined regression coverage and release ordering are shared with ST-101 on the core-payments deployment.
affected_capabilities: Fraud rule versioning and policy signal exposure
requirement.engineering_scope: Small, contained change: one velocity rule added to the existing fraud rule set in fraud-engine, keyed by card token with a sixty-second rolling window and a sixth-attempt block. No new service, endpoint, schema or auth change; payment-service and risk-engine continue to use their existing screening call and policy signal. Main coordination work is rule ordering, combined ST-101/ST-110 regression evidence and agreed core-payments release timing.

findings.text: The change introduces device-bound biometric login and challenge validation, so personal data handling expands into device registration records, challenge artifacts and session establishment for mobile-banking and authentication-service. The exposure is that opt-in registration, revocation and credential fallback are processed across mobile-banking, authentication-service, api-gateway and the encrypted profile store in customer-db, so purpose limitation, lawful basis capture and retention of these new artifacts require review.

Replayed, expired and failed biometric challenges must not yield an authenticated session, and revocation from session settings must stop biometric login from that device. This creates an exposure around how device registration identifiers, challenge outcomes and revocation state are logged or retained, since unnecessary persistence of authentication telemetry can exceed what the feature requires.

Credential fallback for unsupported or failed biometrics keeps existing customer credential flows in scope, and those flows traverse api-gateway and authentication-service. The exposure is that fallback paths may log or transmit personal data differently from the new biometric path, so minimization and masking behaviour across both paths should be checked for consistency.

recommendations: Verify that opt-in consent evidence, revocation propagation and device deregistration are recorded and honoured across mobile-banking and authentication-service, including how the state is reflected for customer-db profile records.

Confirm data minimization, retention and deletion expectations for biometric-derived challenge artifacts, device registration metadata and authentication telemetry held by authentication-service and mobile-banking.

findings.text: The change alters mobile login and session establishment for a channel that reaches financial-processing services, so access controls protecting account-service and payment-service are indirectly in scope even though the story does not describe direct financial-data edits. The exposure is that weakened or inconsistent authentication could affect who can reach payment and account functions.

Authentication events issued by authentication-service and routed through api-gateway may be relied upon as part of the audit trail supporting transaction authorization. The exposure is that failed, expired or replayed challenges, if not consistently logged and rejected, could undermine the completeness of authentication evidence used in financial-control testing.

The story requires authentication-service deployment, shared challenge contract and rollback policy to be scheduled jointly with ST-107 because both changes alter challenge validation. The exposure is change-management and segregation-of-duties evidence for this coordinated deployment, including whether rollback restores the prior authentication policy.

recommendations: Verify that authentication and authorization events from authentication-service and api-gateway are captured completely and immutably in the audit records relied upon for financial-control evidence.

Credential fallback and revocation behaviour affects customer-facing flows that pass through api-gateway, and revocation must reliably stop biometric login from a device. The exposure is that operational monitoring, authorization tests and release evidence may not yet cover revocation propagation and challenge expiry handling across these components.
